answer: Every founding starts on the same mesa, at one measured block, and no seat can mint a peer above it: a second seat must be carved from an existing block, half the carved portion forfeited to the treasury. A lineage of k descendants keeps only one part in two to the k of its founding block, so ten generations leave under a thousandth and twenty under a millionth. The halving spiral repeats each generation, and each cut is recorded in ivory on the ledger, where weight cannot flow back to a parent or sideways to a fresh key. A farm thus needs many independent foundings, each paying its own price.
